findings.F1: The Calmar failure comes from the days the coin closed below its 30-day average price. On those 6,743 coin-days the book's position averaged 0.87 and its gain averaged only 0.031 % a day. On the 6,430 coin-days above that average the position averaged 0.81 and the gain averaged 0.207 % a day. These are hourly gains before costs, with the coin's state read at the first bar of each day.
findings.F2: Rebuilt from those daily gains before costs, the book over all days falls 81 % at its deepest and has a Calmar of 0.34. Kept only on days above the 30-day average, its deepest fall shrinks to 34 %, its yearly return rises from 27.6 % to 37.2 %, its Calmar reaches 1.11 and its Sharpe 1.13. Kept only below it, Calmar is -0.06 and Sharpe 0.13.
findings.F3: The recorded book's deepest fall is 66 % and lasts across many windows: inside the chain it is between 50 % and 64 % in 12 of the 24 windows. Its worst 3 % of days hold 2.9 times the book's whole net gain in losses. The falls are long declines the book stays long through, not one window's accident.
findings.F4: The rebound sits in the deepest falls and is not graded across the rest. On the 2,054 grid cases with a positive forecast, the 72-hour excess return by forecast quartile is -0.03 %, -0.27 %, -0.69 % (t -2.1), then +1.22 % (t 3.5) in the deepest quartile only.
findings.F5: Measured against the coin's own hourly volatility over the last 30 days, the 24-hour fall separates the cases more sharply. The deepest quartile is followed by +1.93 % over 72 hours (t 5.2, 514 cases); the other three quartiles give -0.27 %, +0.32 % and +0.04 %.
findings.F6: The deepest falls rebound most when the coin is above its 30-day average.
findings.F7: As tested, the idea's unusual move is +0.06 % per case, 0.3 times the 0.19 % round-trip cost. In the deepest quartile above the 30-day average, the total move is +2.83 % per case. That is about 15 times the cost, and still several times the cost once the coin's normal drift of about 0.4 % over 72 hours is removed.
findings.F8: The book's 30-day context matters for the forecast itself. The forecast is standardised over its last 60 hours, so it grades a fall against the last 2.5 days, not against the coin's usual volatility. This is why its middle quartiles carry no rebound (F4), while the volatility-scaled fall does (F5).

ideas.idea: The more a coin has fallen over its last 24 hours, the more it rises over the next 3 days, only while its price is above its average price of the last 30 days.
ideas.consequence: A trader buys one-day falls in coins that sit above their 30-day average and refuses them below it, where the long falls that sink the book happen.
ideas.name: dip rebound above trend

ideas.idea: The larger a coin's fall over its last 24 hours relative to its typical hourly moves of the last 30 days, the more it rises over the next 3 days, only while its price is above its average price of the last 30 days.
ideas.consequence: A trader sizes the rebound bet by how unusual the one-day fall is for that coin, which concentrates the position in the cases whose move is many times a round trip.
ideas.name: volatility-scaled dip rebound
